en: The Fundamental Sarvāstivāda Vinaya Sūtra,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree:
This Prātimokṣa Sūtra is difficult to hear, even throughout immeasurable koṭis of kalpas.
Reciting, studying, and upholding [the Dharma] is likewise so; those who practice according to the teaching are even rarer to encounter.
It is a joy for the Buddhas to appear in the world; it is a joy to proclaim the subtle and sublime True Dharma.
It is a joy for the Saṃgha to be of one mind and a single vision; it is a joy to practice together in harmony with courageous diligence.
To see the noble ones is joy; to dwell together with them is also joy.
Not seeing those who are foolish and deluded—this is what is called constantly experiencing happiness.
To see one who is endowed with ethical discipline is happiness; to see one who is learned is also called happiness.
To see an Arhat is true happiness, because of the non-arising of future existence.
There is joy in the delightful stairway at the river’s crossing; there is joy in conquering the battle of enmity through the Dharma.
When the fruit of right wisdom is realized, there is the joy of being able to eliminate the conceit of "I" entirely.
If one can form a resolute intention, well-subduing the senses and desires while possessing great learning;
from youth until old age dwelling in the forest, one finds joy in the quiet seclusion of the araṇya.
"Venerable sirs!

Of the spring season, this much has passed and this much remains. Since old age and death have already encroached, the life-faculty gradually diminishes; the Great Teacher’s Dharma and Vinaya shall soon perish."
"Venerable sirs!

You should diligently manifest [the Dharma] and not be negligent. Through non-negligence, you will certainly realize the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; how much more so the other wholesome dharmas belonging to the category of enlightenment!"
"Venerable Saṃgha! What should be done first?
The Buddha’s community of śrāvakas seeks little and has few concerns."
"Those who have not yet received full ordination must leave.
Those bhikṣus who have not come must announce their *chanda* (consent) and *pariśuddhi* (purity).
Then the one holding the *chanda* said to each person sitting opposite him, "Who has sent the bhikṣuṇī to request instruction?"
With palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas;
this Prātimokṣa of Discipline, I shall now proclaim—listen with virtuous attention.
Having heard it, you should practice correctly, just as the Great Sage has taught.
Regarding even minor transgressions, one should guard them with vigor and diligence.
The horse of the mind is difficult to restrain; it must be governed by constant and resolute application.
The Prātimokṣa is like a bit, possessing a hundred needles of extreme sharpness.
If a person violates the rules of conduct, they can immediately cease upon hearing the teaching;
such a Great Being is like a fine horse who shall emerge from the battle array of afflictions.
If a person lacks this bit, they will likewise never experience joy.
They have perished in the fray of afflictions, wandering deludedly through birth and death.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Today the Saṃgha shall perform the poṣadha on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, or the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now perform the poṣadha and recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra."
"Thus it is declared. "Venerable sirs!
I shall now perform the poṣadha and recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra."
Venerable sirs, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well.
Those who have committed an offense should disclose it; those who have not committed one may remain silent.
By remaining silent, it is known that you, venerable sirs, are pure.
As when questioned at other times, you should answer according to the facts.
Now, within this assembly of superior bhikṣus, even as I ask three times, you should likewise answer according to the facts.
If a bhikṣu remembers that he has committed an offense and does not disclose it, he incurs the offense of intentional lying.
Venerable sirs,
the Buddha has declared that intentional lying is an obstructive dharma.
Therefore, O Bhikṣus, those who seek purity should confess their transgressions.
To confess brings peace and happiness; not to confess brings no peace or happiness.
Venerable sirs!
I have already recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Now I ask the Venerable Ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it is said three times: "Venerable sirs!
Since you are silent, you are pure in this matter; I now hold it thus.
"Venerable sirs!"
"These four *pārājika* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
The summary verse says:
'If one commits an impure act, takes what is not given, or kills a human being;'"
To falsely claim superhuman qualities—these cases all entail non-cohabitation.

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, together with other bhikṣus, has received the training rules, yet does not relinquish those rules nor confess his weakness in training, and commits an act of impurity through sexual intercourse—even with an animal—this bhikṣu also incurs a pārājika offense and shall not cohabit."
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes with a thieving mind an object not given by another;
if at the time of such theft, a king or a high minister should seize him, or kill him, or bind him, or banish him, or reprimand him, saying: 'Ho, man!'"
"You are a thief, deluded and ignorant, to commit such theft.
If a bhikṣu steals in this manner, he too incurs a pārājika offense and shall not live in communion.

“Furthermore, if a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of a human being or a human fetus with his own hand, or provides a weapon, or personally wields a weapon, or seeks one who wields a weapon, or encourages death, or praises death, saying: ‘O man!...’”
"What use is this burdened, impure, and evil life?
It would be better for you to die now; death is superior to life.
Thus, according to his own thoughts, he uses various words to exhort and praise [the victim], urging them toward death.
If that person dies because of it, this bhikṣu also incurs a pārājika offense and shall not live in community with others.

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, being actually without knowledge and without thorough understanding, knowing for himself that he has not attained the state of a superior person, the tranquility of a noble one, or the excellent realization, wisdom, vision, and abiding in bliss, yet says: 'I know; I see.'"
At another time, whether questioned or unasked, desiring to purify himself, he speaks thus:
"Venerable sirs!
It is true that I did not know and did not see, yet I said I knew and I saw; this was a false and deceptive lie."
"Excepting those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), this bhikṣu also incurs a *pārājika* offense and should not live in community.
Venerable sirs, I have now recited the four *pārājika* dharmas; if a bhikṣu commits any one of these acts, he may no longer dwell together with the bhikṣus."
As before, so it is hereafter: having incurred a defeat (*pārājika*), one should not dwell together [with the Sangha].
Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this matter?
Thus he asks three times: "Venerable Ones!"
"In this matter we are pure; because we are silent, I now hold it to be so.
"Venerable sirs!
These thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa dharmas are recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra."
The summary verse says:
Emission, touching, lewdness, and providing offerings; matchmaking, small huts, large monasteries, and slander;
improper acts, causing schism in the Saṃgha, and following along with impure and arrogant speech.
"If again a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, except during a dream, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"If again a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by passion, makes physical contact with the body of a woman—whether grasping her hand, grasping her arm, grasping her hair, or touching any part of her body—with the intent of experiencing pleasure, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
"If again a bhikṣu, with a mind obsessed by defilement, engages in vulgar, evil, and improper speech associated with sexual desire with a woman, as between husband and wife, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"If again a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by passion, should in the presence of a woman praise his own person, saying: 'Sister!

If there were a bhikṣu similar to me—one who is fully endowed with moral discipline (*śīla*), possesses superior wholesome qualities, and practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*)—you should offer this dharma of sexual desire to him.'"
"If a bhikṣu speaks in such a manner, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu acts as a matchmaker, conveying a man's intentions to a woman and a woman's intentions to a man, whether for the purpose of formal marriage or for illicit relations, even for as little as a moment, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu should personally solicit materials to build a small hut for his own use where there is no owner, he must build it according to the prescribed measurements.
Herein, the measurement is twelve spans of the Buddha’s hands in length and seven spans in width."

That bhikṣu should lead the community of bhikṣus to inspect the site; that community of bhikṣus should examine whether the site is appropriate according to the Dharma, a pure place, free from disputes, and a location conducive to spiritual progress.

If a bhikṣu, at an improper and impure site, in a place subject to dispute and lacking access, should personally beg for materials to build a dwelling for himself without a patron and for his own use, and without having other bhikṣus go to inspect the site, and should he construct it there in excess of the prescribed dimensions, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If again a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling for the sake of the Saṃgha with a patron, that bhikṣu should lead a group of bhikṣus to inspect the site.
That group of bhikṣus should inspect the site to ensure it is a proper and pure location, free from disputes, and suitable for spiritual progress."

If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling in an unsuitable location—an impure place, a place of contention, or a place lacking access—and it is for a patron to build for the Saṃgha, yet he does not take other bhikṣus to inspect the site before constructing such a large dwelling, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If again a bhikṣu, harboring anger and not relinquishing it, intentionally slanders a pure bhikṣu with a groundless *pārājika* offense, desiring to ruin that one's pure conduct."
At a later time, whether questioned or unasked, if it is known that this is groundless slander,
and that monk made these statements out of malice, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

“If, moreover, a bhikṣu, harboring ill will and not relinquishing it, intentionally slanders a pure bhikṣu with a groundless accusation of a *pārājika* offense, desiring to ruin that person’s pure conduct;”
At a later time, whether questioned or unasked, knowing this to be a matter that is extraneous and improper, one slanders another by means of a slight resemblance of facts.
If that bhikṣu utters such words out of malice, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu employs means with the intent to split a harmonious Saṃgha, and persists in his adherence to the matter of schism without relinquishing it, [it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense].
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!
Do not persist in your intent to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha."
"Venerable one!

You should live in harmony with the Saṃgha, dwelling together in joy and without dispute; being of one mind and one voice, like water mixed with milk, you shall cause the Teacher’s instruction to shine forth and abide long in peace and happiness."
"Venerable one!
You should relinquish this act of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
When the bhikṣus have thus admonished him, it is well if he relinquishes it.
If he does not relinquish it, one should earnestly and formally admonish him two or three times, and following the instruction, interrogate him so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If, moreover, a bhikṣu—whether one, two, or many—acts as a companion and partisan to that bhikṣu, adhering to what is wrong and opposing what is right, and remains in conformity with him."
Then that bhikṣu said to the other bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
Do not engage in any discussion with that bhikṣu, whether it be regarding what is good or what is bad."
Why is this? Because that bhikṣu conforms to the Dharma and the Vinaya, relies upon the Dharma and the Vinaya, and his speech is free from falsehood.
What he finds delightful, I too find delightful.
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!
Do not speak in this way."
"That bhikṣu accords with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and relies upon the Dharma and the Vinaya; his speech is not false.
What he finds pleasing, I also find pleasing. Why is this?"
That bhikṣu does not conform to the Dharma and Vinaya, nor does he rely upon the Dharma and Vinaya; his words are entirely false and deceptive.

You must not delight in causing a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead delight in harmony with the Saṃgha. You ought to be in accord with the Saṃgha, rejoicing without dispute, with a single mind and a single voice, like water and milk blending together, so that the Great Teacher’s teachings may be made radiant and endure in peace for a long time.
"Venerable one!
You should abandon this evil view of schisming the Saṃgha, which follows what is false and opposes what is right, and cease from persistently maintaining this contentious matter.
If the bhikṣus, when admonished in this manner, abandon it, that is well.

If he does not relinquish it, one should admonish him earnestly and correctly two or three times, and should question him in accordance with the instruction, so as to cause him to relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"Furthermore, if a number of bhikṣus reside in a village or town and defile the families there, engaging in misconduct; and if their defiling of families is seen, heard, and known by many, and their misconduct is also seen, heard, and known by many."
The bhikṣus should say to those bhikṣus:
"Venerable ones!

You have defiled families and committed evil deeds; that you have defiled families is known by the community through seeing, hearing, and awareness, and that you have committed evil deeds is also known by the community through seeing, hearing, and awareness. You should depart; you ought not to remain here."
That bhikṣu said to the other bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs, you possess affection, hatred, fear, and delusion; for there are bhikṣus who have committed such identical offenses, yet some are expelled while others are not."
Then the bhikṣus said to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!
Do not speak such words."
"Venerable sirs, there are [monks] who possess attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; thus, among bhikṣus who have committed identical offenses, some are expelled while others are not."

"Why is this? Because the bhikṣus are free from attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; yet you have defiled families and committed evil deeds. That you defiled families is known by the public through seeing and hearing, and that you committed evil deeds is likewise known by the public through seeing and hearing."
"Venerable ones!
You should abandon such speech as 'love' and 'hatred.
When the bhikṣus have been admonished in this manner, it is well if they abandon it."
If he does not relinquish it, one should earnestly and formally admonish him two or three times, and according to the instruction, interrogate him so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu is of a wicked nature and does not accept the words of others, and when the bhikṣus, in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, offer him counsel regarding the Sūtra of the Precepts spoken by the Buddha, he refuses their admonition and says:
'Venerable sirs!'"
Do not speak even a little to me, whether good or bad; nor shall I speak, whether good or bad, to the venerable ones.
Venerable ones, please desist!
"Do not exhort me; do not speak of me.
Then the bhikṣus said to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!"
Do not refuse to accept admonition. When the bhikṣus exhort you in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya during the recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, you should accept their admonition.
Venerable one, as you exhort the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, the bhikṣus shall likewise exhort you in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, the community of disciples of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha increases and mutually admonishes one another:
"Venerable one,
you should abandon this matter."
When the bhikṣus have admonished him in this manner, it is well if he relinquishes [the matter].

If he does not relinquish it, they should admonish him earnestly and correctly up to three times, and following their instructions, they should interrogate him so as to cause him to relinquish that matter.
"If you abandon it, that is well;
if you do not abandon it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"Venerable sirs!"
I have already explained the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas: nine are offenses incurred immediately, and four are incurred after a third admonition.
If a bhikṣu, having committed any one of these, intentionally conceals it, the Saṃgha shall grant him a *parivāsa* of non-contentment for as many days as he has concealed it.
When the *pārivāsika* (probationary) period has been completed, the community should grant him a six-night *mānāpya* (penance).
When the *mānāpya* has been completed, there remains the removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*); this monk’s offense should be removed in an assembly of twenty monks.
If there is one person missing such that the assembly does not number twenty, the offense of this bhikṣu cannot be removed, and all the bhikṣus incur an offense.
This is the method for the removal of offenses.
"Now I ask the Venerable Ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus he asks three times: "Venerable Ones!"
"In this matter we are pure; because we are silent, I now hold it so.
"Venerable sirs!
These two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharma) are recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra."
The summary verse says:
If one is within a screened enclosure, in a place suitable for sexual intercourse,
or in an unobstructed place where there is no third person present.
"If again a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded place, screened from view and suitable for sexual intercourse, and a faithful upāsikā accuses him of one of three matters:
either a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika offense."
If that seated bhikṣu confesses his own matter, he should be dealt with according to one of the three rules:
either a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*; or he may be dealt with according to the matter as stated by the *upāsikā*. This is called an indeterminate rule (*aniyata-dharma*).
"If again a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a place that is not screened off and is unfit for sexual intercourse, and a faithful upāsikā states to him one of two rules—
either a saṃghāvaśeṣa or a pāyattika."
If that seated bhikṣu confesses his own matter, he should be dealt with according to one of two rules:
either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*; or he may be dealt with according to the matter as described by the *upāsikā*. This is called an indeterminate rule (*aniyata-dharma*).
"Venerable sirs!
I have already recited the two rules of undetermined offense.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: [Are you pure in this matter?]"
"Is there purity in this matter?
Thus he asks three times: "Venerable sirs!
Since there is silence, there is purity in this matter; thus do I now hold it."
"Venerable sirs!
These thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
The initial summary verse says:"
Holding, parting from, storing, and washing robes;
taking robes, begging for them, receiving more than allowed, equal value, and different owners; sending a messenger to deliver the price for a robe.
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and the kaṭhina period has ended, he may keep an extra robe for up to ten days without having formally designated it."
If one keeps [the robe] beyond that limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and the *kaṭhina* period has ended, he should not stay overnight—down to a single night—outside the boundary of any one of the three robes, except by means of a formal act of the Saṃgha; otherwise, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and the kaṭhina robe has been suspended, and he obtains an out-of-season robe, he may accept it if he needs it.

Having accepted it, he should quickly have it made into a robe; if there is hope for obtaining more to complete it, he may seek to fulfill that need. If it is still insufficient, he may keep it for up to one month."
If he exceeds [the limit], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or beat an old robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu should take a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu should beg for a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, except at other times, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
Regarding the "exceptional circumstances": if a bhikṣu’s robes have been snatched away, lost, burned, blown away, or carried off by water—this is the appropriate time.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu’s robes have been snatched away, lost, burned, blown away, or carried off by water, he may beg for robes from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative. If they offer many robes, the bhikṣu, if he has need, should accept only two robes: one upper robe and one lower robe.
If one accepts more than that, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"Furthermore, if a monk, there are a householder and a householder’s wife who are not relatives, who together provide the price for a robe, intending: 'We shall buy such a pure robe and give it to a certain monk for him to use at the proper time.'"
This bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation, upon being informed by another, went to that person's house and spoke these words: "Excellent!
O worthy one, you have prepared the price for a robe for my sake; you may purchase such a pure robe and give it to me in a timely manner, so that it may be of good quality."
If he should obtain the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"Furthermore, if a monk, there are a householder and a householder’s wife who are not kinsmen, and each has prepared the price for a robe, intending to buy such a pure robe and give it to a certain monk."
This bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation, was informed by another and went to that person's house, saying: "Excellent!
O worthy one, you have prepared the price for a robe for my sake; you should purchase such a pure robe with it and give it to me in a timely manner, so that it may be of good quality."
If he should obtain the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if a king, a great minister, a brahmin, a householder, or others should send a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to a bhikṣu:
That messenger, taking the price for the robe to where the bhikṣu was, said to him:
"Venerable One!
This item has been sent by such-and-such a king, minister, brahmin, or householder, and I have been dispatched to deliver it."
"Venerable sir!
Out of compassion, please accept it.
Then that bhikṣu said to the messenger:
"Venerable sir, I should not accept this price for robes;
if I obtain a pure robe that is appropriate for the season, I shall accept it.
The messenger then said:
"Venerable One!
Is there anyone who manages affairs?
The bhikṣu in need of robes said:
"There is! Whether it be a monastery attendant (śrāmaṇera) or an upāsaka, these are the monks' attendants.
That messenger goes to the attendant and, having given him the price for the robe, says:
"You may take this price for robes and purchase a timely, pure robe to give to the bhikṣu so-and-so, so that he may wear it.
After that messenger has properly instructed the attendant, he returns to the bhikṣu and says:
"Venerable One!..."
"The person in charge you indicated, I have already provided with the price for robes; he shall receive pure robes.
When a bhikṣu requires robes, he should go to the person in charge and, after reminding them two or three times, say:
"I require robes."
"If he obtains them, it is well;
if he does not obtain them, he should go to that place silently and remain wherever he is for a fourth, fifth, or sixth time.
If he obtains the robe after the fourth, fifth, or sixth time, it is well."
If he does not obtain the robe and continues to seek it beyond this limit, and thereby obtains the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he still does not obtain the robe at all, that bhikṣu should go to the place where the robe-price was sent, either going himself or sending a trustworthy person, and announce:
"The robe-price was sent by you for the sake of a certain bhikṣu; however, that bhikṣu did not ultimately obtain the robe."
“O Benevolent One, you should know this and not let it be lost;
now is the time.
The second summary verse says:
Kauśeya silk that is purely black; dividing the six *niṣīdana* mats;
carrying wool; washing gold and silver; taking a pledge; and buying and selling.
"If a bhikṣu should use new *kauśeya* silk thread to make a bedding mat (*pariṣkāra*), it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding out of pure black sheep’s wool, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu makes a new sheep’s wool bedding, he should use two parts of pure black, a third part of white, and a fourth part of coarse wool."

If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat without using two parts of pure black wool, one-third part of white wool, and one-fourth part of coarse wool, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat, even if his heart is not inclined toward it, he should use it for six years.
If he does not discard the old one after less than six years and makes another new one—unless he has obtained the formal authorization of the Saṃgha—he commits a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense."

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu makes a new *niṣīdana*, he should take a piece from the worn portion of an old one, measuring one span of the Buddha’s hand in length and breadth, and patch it onto the new one for the purpose of discoloring it."
If a bhikṣu makes a new *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) and does not patch the old one onto the new one for the purpose of discoloring it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains wool while traveling on a road and has need of it, he may take it.
If there is no one to carry it for him, he may carry it himself for up to three yojanas."
If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu should have a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu should take gold, silver, coins, or the like with his own hand, or instruct another to take them, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.

"If a bhikṣu again engages in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
The third summary verse says:
Two bowls, two weavers, taking away robes, and urgent offerings.
Rain-clothing for forest-dwellers, and medicine for seven days diverted from the Saṃgha.
"If a bhikṣu again keeps an extra alms-bowl beyond ten days without making a formal distribution, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."

That bhikṣu shall relinquish this bowl in the midst of the community; the community shall take the lowest-quality bowl from among its own bowls and give it to that bhikṣu, saying:

"If a robe is separated from that person's body and one uses it for oneself, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Furthermore, if many bhikṣus are staying in a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*) for the later retreat (*paścima-varṣā*), and there is a place of fear, terror, or danger, a bhikṣu may, from among his three robes (*tricīvara*), leave one robe behind in a village dwelling.

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object intended for the Saṃgha has been given, diverts it for his own personal use, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu consumes [it] beyond seven days, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, should speak of it to one who is not yet fully ordained—except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha—it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, having actually attained the state of a superior person (uttaramanuṣyadharma), should speak of it to one who has not yet received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.

The second summary verse says:
Seeds, disparaging, and instructing; placing beds, grass mats, and pulling.

"If a bhikṣu himself destroys a village of seeds or sentient beings, or causes another to destroy it, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, moreover, should disparage, revile, or treat another bhikṣu with contempt, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, moreover, should disobey or annoy [another] regarding their verbal instruction, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣu places monastic bedding or various seats in an open area and departs without putting them away himself, nor instructing another to put them away, and if there is no other bhikṣu to whom he has entrusted them—except in cases of other extenuating circumstances—it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣu, within a monastery dwelling, spreads grass or leaves himself or instructs another to spread them, and upon departing neither removes them himself nor instructs another to remove them, and if there is no other bhikṣu to whom he has entrusted the care of them—unless there is a special reason—this is a pāyattika."
"If again a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, drags a bhikṣu out of a monastery dwelling, or causes another to drag him out, except for other extenuating circumstances, it is a pāyattika."

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, in a monastery dwelling, knowing that other bhikṣus have previously resided there, later arrives and intentionally causes them annoyance or offense by sitting or lying down upon their bedding, thinking:

Pāyattika: "If a bhikṣu, in a dwelling belonging to the Saṃgha, knowing that it is a multi-storied building with an upper loft, should sit or lie down carelessly on a bed with removable legs or other seating furniture, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living beings, pours it over grass or soil, or mixes it with cow dung, or instructs another to do so, it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling, he should install a crossbar at the side of the door-post, as well as windows and drainage outlets.
When building the walls, if they are made of wet clay, they should be built two or three stories high, level with the position of the crossbar."
If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *pāyattika*.

Not being appointed, until sunset, for the sake of food, and two kinds of robes.
Traveling on the same road or by boat, and eating while both are secluded from the view of others—these constitute the training rules for food.
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, without being dispatched by the Saṃgha, goes of his own accord to instruct a bhikṣuṇī, except when he has attained a superior dharma, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, although appointed by the community to instruct bhikṣuṇīs, should provide instruction until the time of sunset, it is a pāyattika."

...so it is a *pāyattika*.
"If again a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu travels together with a bhikṣuṇī as part of a caravan, except during other [permitted] times, it is a pāyattika."
"Other times" refers to occasions when there is fear or danger; these are considered appropriate times.
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to ride in the same boat, whether going downstream or upstream—except for a direct crossing—it is a pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣu should again sit in a secluded place alone with a woman, it is a pāyattika.

Eating frequently; staying one night; accepting alms bowls and not for the sake of others;
being satisfied with food; eating separately at improper times; and touching exquisite food that has not been formally accepted.

"If a bhikṣu stays for even one night and takes one meal at the dwelling place of non-Buddhists, except when there is a cause such as illness;

Once one has received it and returned to the residence, if there are other bhikṣus present, they should share the food together; this is the proper time.

"If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu [should eat] such excellent foods as milk,
curd, fresh butter, fish, and meat, as spoken of by the Blessed One:..."

"If a bhikṣu should give food with his own hand to a naked ascetic or to any other male or female non-Buddhist practitioner, it is a pāyattika.

"Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One.

"You should abandon such an evil view.

if he does not abandon it, it is a *pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu knows that such a person has not yet acted in accordance with the Dharma and has not abandoned his evil view..."
"To engage in conversation with them, to dwell together with them in shared enjoyment, or to sleep in the same room as them, constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

The bhikṣus should say to that śrāmaṇera:
"Do not speak these words:
'I understand what the Buddha has taught—that those things which are obstructive dharmas are not obstructions when one practices them.'"
"Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One.

"You should abandon such an evil view.

Killing animals and causing distress, Prodding, tickling, and sleeping in the same place as water;

"If a bhikṣu himself hides the robes, bowl, or other requisites of a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, or causes another to hide them, except for other circumstances, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe entrusted to him by another, later wears it himself without asking the owner, it is a pāyattika.

"If again a bhikṣu travels along the same road with a woman, without another man present, even for the distance between two villages, it is a pāyattika."

Robbers, age not yet reached, digging the earth, invitations, violating the instructions,
eavesdropping, departing in silence, lack of respect, alcohol, and untimely food.

"If a bhikṣu receives an invitation for four months, he should accept it when necessary.

The exceptions are: a special invitation, a repeated invitation, a cordial invitation, and a regular invitation; these are the appropriate times.

"If a bhikṣu again fails to show respect, it is a pāyattika.

Eating, the appearance of dawn, and now knowing; needle cases, bed-leg measurements.
Storing flowers and sitting mats; the rain and the Master’s robe.

If one makes it exceeding [the prescribed measure], it should be cut down; it is a *pāyattika*.
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in measure to the Buddha’s robe, or exceeds it, it is a *pāyattika*."
"Regarding the measurement of the Buddha’s robe herein: it is ten spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and six spans in width;
this is the measurement of the Buddha’s robe. "O Venerable Ones!

Since you are pure in this matter and remain silent, I now hold it to be so.

The summary verse says:
Receiving from a nun who is not a relative, and eating food assigned in a house."
One must not go uninvited to a family home to receive food outside the monastery.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, while on a village road, receives food with his own hands from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and eats it, [he commits an offense].
That bhikṣu should return to the residence outside the village, go to where the other bhikṣus are, and address each of them individually, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
I have committed a fault that requires confession; it was improper for me to do so, and I now confess it before you."
This is called the "Method of Responding with Speech.

Furthermore, if many bhikṣus are eating at the home of a layperson and a bhikṣuṇī gives instructions, saying, "This bhikṣu should be given much fine food and drink," [the bhikṣus should respond accordingly].
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister, please wait for a short while until the bhikṣus have finished eating."
If not a single person speaks these words, those bhikṣus should return to their residence outside the village, go to where the other bhikṣus are, and each address them individually, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"I have committed a fault that requires confession; this was not what I ought to have done, and I now confess it before you.
This is called a "dharma requiring confession.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu knows that a family is under the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the disciplinary rite of being placed under training) by the Saṃgha, and if the bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation, goes to that house and eats food with his own hands, [he commits an offense].
That bhikṣu should return to the residence outside the village, go to where the other bhikṣus are, and address each of them individually, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
I have committed an offense of confession, which was improper to do; I now confess it before you."
This is called the "Instruction for a Specific Case.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu dwells in a forest hermitage that is a place of fear and danger, and if there is no one beforehand to scout for perils, yet he accepts food outside his dwelling and eats it, that bhikṣu must return to his dwelling, go to where the other bhikṣus are, and address each of them individually, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."

"These are the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma), which are recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
A summary verse says:
"Regarding food, clothing, and physical deportment, one should maintain proper decorum when visiting the homes of the laity."
One should protect one’s bowl, except in the case of a sick person; [one should avoid] grass, water, and trees taller than a person.
One should train oneself to wear the lower robe (saṃghāṭī) neatly.
One should train oneself to wear the lower robe neither too high nor too low, not like an elephant’s trunk, not like a snake’s head, not like a *tāla* leaf, and not in the shape of a bean cake.
"One should train oneself to wear the three robes neatly and properly.

One should train oneself to enter the houses of laypeople without wearing them too high or too low, but rather wearing them well-adjusted and well-covered, speaking little, and not looking about with upraised eyes."

"One should train oneself: not to enter the homes of laypeople with the head covered, nor with the robe tucked up on one side, nor with the robe tucked up on both sides, nor with hands on the hips, nor by slapping the shoulders."
"One should train oneself: when entering the homes of laypeople, one shall not walk crouching, nor walk on tiptoe, nor walk leaping, nor walk with feet splayed, nor walk with the body hunched."

"One should train oneself thus: 'I shall enter the house of a layperson without swaying the body, without swinging the arms, without shaking the head, without jostling with the shoulders, and without joining hands.'"
"One should train oneself: 'In the house of a layperson, one should not sit down without being invited to do so.
One should train oneself: 'In the house of a layperson, one should not sit down without having carefully observed [the surroundings].'"
"One should train oneself: 'In the house of a layperson, one shall not sit with the body unrestrained.

One should train oneself: 'In the house of a layperson, one shall not cross the legs, nor overlap the inner ankles, nor overlap the outer ankles; one shall not draw the feet too tightly together, nor extend the feet too far, nor expose the body.'"
"One should train oneself to receive food with reverence.

One must not receive rice in a bowl so full that when soup and vegetables are added, they overflow the rim; one should leave space for the fingers and receive the food with care. Thus should one train."
"One should train oneself: 'When the food has not yet arrived, one shall not extend the bowl in advance.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not place the bowl atop the food.
One should train oneself: 'One shall eat with reverence.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not take a mouthful that is too small, nor one that is too large; I shall eat with the mouthful rounded and compact.
One should train oneself: 'If food has not yet reached my mouth, I shall not open my mouth to wait for it.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not speak while eating.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not cover the soup or vegetables with rice, nor shall I cover the rice with soup or vegetables, lest I expect to receive more.'"

"One should train oneself not to eat by clicking the tongue, not to eat by smacking the lips, not to eat by making hissing sounds, not to eat by blowing on the food, not to eat with scattered hands, not to disparage the food, not to stuff the cheeks, not to bite off half-bites, not to lick the hands or tongue, and not to form the food into the shape of a *stūpa*."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not lick my hands; I shall not lick my bowl; I shall not shake my hands; I shall not shake my bowl;
I shall always look at my own bowl while eating. One should train oneself: 'I shall not look into the bowl of a fellow monk with a disrespectful mind.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not grasp the pure water vessel with soiled hands.
One should train oneself: 'In the house of a layperson, I shall not discard the rinsing water from my bowl, except after asking the host.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not place leftover food into the water of the alms bowl.
One should train oneself: 'One must not set down the alms bowl on the ground without a base.
One should train oneself: 'One must not wash the alms bowl while standing.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not place my bowl on a precarious bank, nor shall I scoop water against the current.
One should train oneself: 'Unless one is ill, I shall not preach the Dharma while standing to a person who is seated.'"
"One should train oneself: unless the person is ill, one shall not preach the Dharma while sitting to someone who is lying down.
One should train oneself: unless the person is ill, one shall not preach the Dharma while seated on a lower seat to someone who is on a higher seat."
"One should train oneself: 'If another person is walking ahead and I am walking behind, I shall not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'If another person is on the path and I am off the path, I shall not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.'"

"One should train oneself: except in the case of illness, one must not teach the Dharma to those who have their heads covered, those who have tucked up one side of their robe, those who have tucked up both sides of their robe, those who have their hands on their hips, or those who are slapping their shoulders."

"One should train oneself: except in the case of illness, one shall not preach the Dharma to those riding elephants, nor to those riding horses, nor to those in palanquins, nor to those in carriages."
"One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to those wearing wooden clogs, boots, shoes, or sandals.

One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to those wearing hats or crowns, nor to those with topknots, nor to those with wrapped heads, nor to those wearing flower ornaments.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not teach the Dharma to one who is wearing a sunshade.
One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not stand while urinating or defecating.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except when ill, one must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate in water.
One should train oneself: 'Except when ill, one must not discard feces, urine, spittle, or expectoration upon green grass.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not climb a tree taller than a person, except when there is a reason for difficulty.
Venerable sirs, I have now recited the numerous rules of training."

Are you pure in this matter?

"In this matter, we are pure, as indicated by our silence; thus do I now hold it.

"Patience is the supreme among ascetic practices; it can lead to the state of Nirvāṇa.
One who causes distress to others while claiming to have left the household life is not called a śramaṇa.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin.
As one with clear eyes avoids dangerous paths and can reach a place of safety,
so the wise person within the realm of birth can distance themselves from all evils.
This is the Sūtra of Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Śikhin.
Neither reviling nor harming, Guarding the Sūtra of Precepts well;
Knowing moderation in food and drink, Using humble bedding and seats;
Diligently cultivating higher concentration— This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
This is the Sūtra of the Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata Viśvabhū, the Perfectly Awakened One:
"Just as a bee gathers nectar from flowers, Without destroying their color or fragrance, But taking only the flavor and departing; So should a bhikṣu enter a village."
This is the Sūtra of Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda:
Do not oppose others; do not look at what they have done or left undone.
But examine your own conduct alone, whether it be right or wrong.
This is the Sūtra of Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kanakamuni:
Do not be attached to a concentrated mind; Diligently cultivate a state of tranquility.
The savior is free from sorrow; Always ensure that mindfulness is not lost.
If one can practice giving, merit increases and enmity subsides of its own accord;
by cultivating goodness one eliminates all evils, and when delusions are exhausted, one reaches Nirvana.
This is the Sūtra of Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa.
Commit no evil in any way; cultivate all that is wholesome;
thoroughly discipline your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
To guard the body is excellent!
To guard speech is good;
to guard the mind is excellent!
To guard them all is supreme.
A bhikṣu who guards all [the sense faculties] can liberate himself from all suffering;
he well guards his speech and also well guards his mind.
He commits no evil with the body and constantly purifies these three types of action.
This is that which can accord with the path practiced by the Great Sage.
This is the Sūtra on the Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, [Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa]...
Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and the Honored One Śākyamuni—
such are the Gods among Gods, the Unsurpassed Tamer of Men.
These seven Buddhas are all heroic and fierce, capable of rescuing and protecting the world.
Those endowed with great renown all proclaim this Dharma of the precepts;
the Buddhas and their disciples alike revere and honor the precepts,
and because they venerate the Sūtra of the Precepts, they attain the unsurpassed fruit.
You should seek liberation and diligently practice the Buddha’s teaching;
subdue the army of birth and death as an elephant destroys a thatched hut.
Within this Dharma and Vinaya, always remain heedful.
One who can exhaust the ocean of afflictions shall reach the end of suffering.
For this purpose the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra is recited; together we perform the *Poṣadha*.
We should all together revere the precepts, as the yak cow cherishes its tail.
I have finished reciting the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; the Saṃgha has completed the Poṣadha ceremony.
May the merit and blessings benefit all sentient beings, so that together they may attain the Way of the Buddha.
